steps: Build the nested list with two rows and three columns.
Print the values so the grouping is visible.
Print `a.shape` and confirm it is `(2, 3)`.
Shape travels with the data.realWorld: A feature matrix read from a CSV must arrive as (rows, features), and the shape is the first thing a model checks.
mistakes: Passing a flat list and expecting rows to appear.
revision: Shape is metadata stored with the array.
Print shape beside values when debugging.

Subtraction and multiplication are eleme.syntax: a - b  ·  a * b  # position by position
steps: Create two arrays with the same shape.
Subtract them and print the result.
Multiply them and compare with a matrix product using `@`.
Subtraction and multiplication are eleme.realWorld: Residuals in a regression are one elementwise subtraction of prediction from target.
mistakes: Reading `*` as a matrix product; that is `@`.
revision: Shapes must be compatible before values are read.

steps: Create a string array from a list of names.
Print the dtype and confirm the `<U` width.
Reverse and print the array with a slice.
An array of strings is still an array.realWorld: Category labels often live in a string array before they are encoded for a model.
mistakes: Trying arithmetic on text without converting it first.
revision: Strings use a fixed-width Unicode dtype.
Slicing and sorting work; arithmetic needs a cast.

tolist detaches the result.syntax: values = a.tolist()  # plain Python list, no shared buffer
steps: Create a small array.
Convert it with `tolist()`.
Change the list and print the array to prove they are separate.
tolist detaches the result.realWorld: APIs and JSON serialisers accept plain lists, so `tolist()` is the hand-off at the boundary.
mistakes: Expecting a mutation of the list to update the array.

steps: Compare an array with a threshold.
Store the result in a variable.
Count the True values with `sum()`.
A boolean result is a normal array.visual:
marks   [35 72 48 90]
mask    [F  T  F  T]
sum     2
A boolean result is a normal array.realWorld: Pass rates and alert counts are boolean arrays reduced to a number.
mistakes: Using the mask as a scalar without reducing it.
revision: Comparisons return a bool array of the same shape.
True counts as 1 in a sum.

steps: Build a 3×2 nested list.
Print its shape to confirm two axes.
Reshape to 2×3 and print the values.
Reshaping a list of lists.realWorld: Image batches are reshaped from a flat buffer into (batch, height, width) before a model.
mistakes: Reshaping to a size that does not multiply to the same count.
revision: Nested lists already carry row structure.
A reshape keeps the values and changes the grouping.

strides report bytes per axis step.syntax: a.strides  # bytes to advance one index on each axis
steps: Create an int64 matrix with `arange` and `reshape`.
Print `a.strides` and `a.shape`.
Move one row and confirm the byte jump matches the row stride.
strides report bytes per axis step.visual:
shape (2, 3), int64
strides (24, 8)
row step 24 bytes = 3 × 8
strides report bytes per axis step.realWorld: Memory layout explains why a transpose is free and why some library calls copy.
mistakes: Reading strides as element counts instead of bytes.
revision: Strides are byte offsets per axis.
C-order rows jump by the row width.

A transpose keeps the same size.syntax: a.T  # shape and strides swap, size is unchanged
steps: Build a 2×3 array.
Print `a.T.shape` and `a.size`.
Compare the strides of both views.
A transpose keeps the same size.realWorld: Linear algebra libraries expect a particular orientation, and transpose supplies it without a copy.
mistakes: Mutating a transpose and being surprised the source changed.
revision: Size is the product of the shape and does not change.

steps: Create one integer and one float array.
Print the full dtype name for both.
Print `.kind` and compare the single letters.
dtype name versus dtype kind.realWorld: Validation code branches on kind when any integer width is acceptable.
mistakes: Comparing `.kind` with the full dtype string.
revision: The name includes width and precision.
The kind is the type family.

steps: Create an array with a zero-length axis.
Print shape, size and nbytes.
Reduce it and observe the empty result.
size is zero when any axis is zero.realWorld: A filter that matches no rows still flows through a pipeline as a valid empty result.
mistakes: Assuming the non-zero axis still yields elements.
revision: One zero axis empties the array.

steps: Build a contiguous matrix.
Print its C, Fortran and writeable flags.
Transpose it and print the flags again.
flags report the memory layout.visual:
a     C True  F False
a.T   C False F True
flags report the memory layout.realWorld: A library that needs contiguous input reads these flags before deciding to copy.
mistakes: Ignoring a non-contiguous warning until a copy appears in profiling.
revision: Flags describe the buffer, not the values.

base links a view to its source.syntax: a[1:3].base is a  # True for a view
steps: Create a vector.
Print `a.base` for the owner and for a slice.
Confirm the slice's base is the source array.
base links a view to its source.realWorld: Debugging a silent data change starts by checking whether two names share a base.
mistakes: Assuming a slice always owns its own data.
revision: A view's base points at the owner.

steps: Pass a vector to `np.diag` and print the square matrix.
Pass a matrix and print the extracted diagonal.
Compare the two shapes.
diag builds a matrix from a vector.realWorld: Covariance matrices and scaling operators are built from a diagonal vector.
mistakes: Forgetting that a 1-D input produces a matrix, not a diagonal.
revision: The input rank decides the direction.
Values off the diagonal are zero.

steps: Create a matrix of ones.
Apply `tril` and print it.
Apply `triu` with an offset and compare.
tril and triu keep one triangle.realWorld: A correlation matrix is often read as its lower triangle to avoid duplicate pairs.
mistakes: Assuming the operation edits the original matrix.
revision: Both return a new array by default.

steps: Repeat a short vector a fixed number of times.
Print the result and its length.
Repeat with per-element counts.
repeat repeats each element.realWorld: Expanding a per-group label to match the rows of each group is a repeat operation.
mistakes: Confusing repeat with tile and getting the wrong grouping.
revision: Output length is the sum of counts.

steps: Tile a short vector twice.
Print the result and check the order.
Tile a column block along the second axis.
tile repeats the whole block.visual:
[1 2] tiled 2 → [1 2 1 2]
block repeated as a unit
tile repeats the whole block.realWorld: Periodic patterns and repeated feature blocks are built with tile.
mistakes: Using tile when each value itself should repeat.
revision: Output length multiplies by the repeat count.

steps: Ask for three values from 10⁰ to 10².
Print them and check the ratio.
Change the base and compare.
logspace spaces powers of ten.realWorld: Learning-rate sweeps and frequency grids are sampled on a log scale.
mistakes: Expecting equal differences between consecutive values.
revision: Spacing is constant in the exponent.
The ratio between neighbours is fixed.

steps: Define a function of row and column index.
Pass it with the desired shape.
Print the grid and verify one cell by hand.
fromfunction builds from indices.realWorld: Coordinate grids for plots and physics simulations come from index formulas.
mistakes: Writing a scalar-only function that cannot take index arrays.

steps: Create a small int8 array.
Cast it to int64 and print both dtypes.
Compare the values to confirm nothing changed.
Casting to a wider type is lossless.realWorld: IDs read from a compact file are widened before arithmetic can overflow.
mistakes: Casting down and assuming NumPy will raise instead of wrapping.

steps: Build a boolean array.
Cast it to int and print the values.
Sum the result to count True cells.
Booleans cast back to integers.realWorld: Flags stored as booleans become 0/1 features for a model.
mistakes: Multiplying a mask by a float array and being unsure of the dtype.
revision: True maps to 1 and False to 0.

steps: Create the same value as float32 and float64.
Print both and compare the decimals.
Check the dtype of each.
float32 keeps fewer digits.realWorld: GPUs prefer float32, so the precision loss is a deliberate trade in training.
mistakes: Accumulating millions of float32 values and trusting the last digits.
revision: float32 has about seven significant digits.

steps: Print the int8 bounds with `iinfo`.
Add 1 to the maximum value.
Observe the wrapped result.
int8 has a small range.realWorld: Quantised models pack weights into int8, so range checks are part of the contract.
mistakes: Using int8 for counters that can exceed 127.

steps: Create a float array.
Cast it with the short code `f4`.
Cast again with a full dtype name and compare.
astype accepts a dtype string.realWorld: Configuration files store dtypes as short strings, so the parser is part of the API.
mistakes: Typing an invalid code and expecting a silent fallback.
revision: String codes are resolved by NumPy.

steps: Ask for the promotion of int8 and int16.
Ask for float32 and int64.
Compare with the dtype of a mixed expression.
promote_types compares two dtypes.visual:
int8 + int16 → int16
float32 + int64 → float64
promote_types compares two dtypes.realWorld: Knowing the promoted dtype prevents a surprising upcast and a large copy.
mistakes: Assuming an int and a float stay integer.
revision: Promotion picks the smallest type holding both.
Mixed arithmetic follows the same rule.

Negative row index selects from the end.syntax: a[-1]  ·  a[-2]  # rows counted from the end
steps: Build a 3×2 matrix.
Print the last row with `a[-1]`.
Print the row before it with `a[-2]`.
Negative row index selects from the end.visual:
a[-1] → last row
a[-2] → second last
Negative row index selects from the end.realWorld: Reading the latest record from a growing table uses the last row.
mistakes: Using `-0` and expecting the last row.
revision: Negative indexes count from the end.
The magnitude must fit the axis length.

steps: Create a (2, 3, 4) array with `arange`.
Print one scalar with three indexes.
Print a 2-D slice and note its shape.
Index a three-dimensional array.realWorld: Image stacks and video frames are indexed by frame, row and column.
mistakes: Forgetting a colon and silently dropping an axis.

Select rows with a boolean list.syntax: a[[True, False, True]]  # keep flagged rows
steps: Build a 3-row matrix.
Pass a boolean list of length 3.
Verify the selected rows and their order.
Select rows with a boolean list.visual:
flags [T F T]
rows 0 and 2 returned
Select rows with a boolean list.realWorld: A split mask selects the training rows of a table.
mistakes: Passing a list whose length is not the row count.
revision: Boolean lists act as masks on the first axis.

steps: Build a matrix.
Call `take` with row positions and `axis=0`.
Print the returned rows in the requested order.
take along rows.realWorld: Reordering a batch by an index array is a take operation.
mistakes: Omitting the axis and flattening the matrix.

steps: Build a matrix.
Index it with an empty list.
Print the shape and size of the empty result.
Index with an empty list.realWorld: A filter with no matches should return an empty table, not an error.
mistakes: Treating an empty selection as a failed query.
revision: An empty index gives an empty axis.

steps: Build a matrix.
Print both column forms and their shapes.
Broadcast each against a row to see the difference.
Read a column as a column.realWorld: Keeping a feature as a column is required before subtracting a per-row value.
mistakes: Using the 1-D form in an outer operation by accident.
revision: A list index keeps the axis.

steps: Create a vector from 0 to 5.
Slice with a negative start and stop.
Print the tail with an open stop.
Slice with a negative start.realWorld: Keeping the last two readings of a sensor stream uses a negative slice.
mistakes: Expecting the stop index to be included.
revision: Negative bounds count from the end.

steps: Build a (2, 3, 4) array.
Slice the middle axis and print the shape.
Slice a single depth and column, then compare.
Slice a three-dimensional array.realWorld: Extracting one channel from an image batch is a middle-axis slice.
mistakes: Mixing the axis order and selecting the wrong channel.
revision: The remaining axes give the output shape.

steps: Create a vector.
Assign zero to a middle slice.
Print the array to confirm only that range changed.
Assign a scalar to a slice.realWorld: Clearing a padded region of a batch is a slice assignment.
mistakes: Using a copy and expecting the source to change.
revision: A basic slice writes into the buffer.
Every view of that buffer sees the change.

steps: Create a zero vector.
Assign a two-value array to a slice of length two.
Print the result and try a mismatched shape.
Assign an array to a slice.visual:
slice length 2 ← array length 2
mismatch raises ValueError
Assign an array to a slice.realWorld: Filling a column range from a computed vector is a routine preprocessing step.
mistakes: Assigning a longer array to a shorter slice.
revision: Values are copied into the destination.

steps: Create a vector.
Print the tail from index 3.
Print a full slice and confirm it is a view.
Slice with an omitted stop.realWorld: Skipping a header row is `a[1:]`, the most common tail slice.
mistakes: Assuming an omitted stop copies the data.
revision: An omitted stop means the axis length.
A full slice is still a view.

steps: Build a matrix with four columns.
Slice alternate columns.
Print the shape to confirm two columns remain.
Slice every other column.realWorld: Dropping every second feature during a quick experiment uses a step slice.
mistakes: Putting the step on the row axis by mistake.
revision: A step belongs to one axis.
The result is a strided view.

steps: Create a flat range of six values.
Reshape to 2×3 and print it.
Reshape to 3×2 and compare the grouping.
reshape groups values in C order.realWorld: A flat image buffer becomes a height-by-width array through a C-order reshape.
mistakes: Expecting column-major fill without `order='F'`.
revision: C order fills the last axis fastest.
The element count must stay the same.

steps: Build a contiguous matrix.
Flatten it with `ravel`.
Check sharing with `shares_memory`.
ravel returns a flat view.realWorld: Passing a matrix to a flat API can avoid a copy when ravel returns a view.
mistakes: Mutating the ravel result and forgetting it may be a view.
revision: Ravel copies only when it must.

steps: Build a matrix.
Flatten it and mutate the result.
Print the source to prove it did not change.
flatten returns a copy.visual:
flatten → independent copy
source stays the same
flatten returns a copy.realWorld: A helper that mutates its input receives `flatten()` to keep the caller's data safe.
mistakes: Using flatten in a hot loop and paying for a copy each time.
revision: The result is independent of the source.

steps: Create two blocks with the same row count.
Concatenate them along axis 1.
Print the resulting shape.
concatenate along columns.realWorld: Adding an engineered feature column to a design matrix is a column concatenation.
mistakes: Joining blocks with different row counts.
revision: The named axis is the one that grows.

steps: Create a length-6 vector.
Split it into three parts and print them.
Try a length that does not divide evenly.
split into equal parts.visual:
len 6 / 3 → three parts of 2
len 7 / 3 → array_split only
split into equal parts.realWorld: Mini-batches are slices or splits of a shuffled index array.
mistakes: Using split when the length is not divisible.

steps: Create a (2, 3, 4) array.
Transpose with an explicit axis order.
Print the new shape and verify one value.
transpose a three-dimensional array.realWorld: Frameworks differ on channel-first versus channel-last, and transpose bridges them.
mistakes: Assuming transpose reverses all axes in 3-D.
revision: The argument is the new axis order.

steps: Create two vectors of equal length.
Apply `maximum` and print the winners.
Compare with a fixed clamp using `clip`.
maximum picks elementwise winners.realWorld: A per-row floor stored as an array is applied with maximum.
mistakes: Using Python's `max` on whole arrays instead of elementwise.

steps: Create two vectors.
Apply `minimum` and print the smaller values.
Use a limit array to cap a result.
minimum pairs the same way.realWorld: Capping predicted probabilities by a per-class threshold uses minimum.
mistakes: Forgetting that broadcasting can change the result shape.
revision: It is the array counterpart of a cap.

steps: Divide a vector containing zero by zero.
Observe the warning and the inf/nan values.
Guard the denominator with a mask.
divide warns on zero.realWorld: Ratios computed from counts hit zero denominators, so the guard is part of the metric.
mistakes: Ignoring the warning until NaNs reach a mean.
revision: Division by zero returns inf or nan.

steps: Create a base and an exponent array.
Apply `power` and print the result.
Compare with the `**` operator.
power raises elementwise.realWorld: Polynomial features are powers of one column with a fixed exponent.
mistakes: Using a negative integer exponent on an integer base.
revision: Exponents are broadcast with the base.

steps: Compute a length with `hypot`.
Compare it with `sqrt(x**2 + y**2)`.
Try large values where the naive form overflows.
hypot is a stable length.realWorld: Distances between coordinates are computed with hypot to avoid overflow.
mistakes: Squaring large values before taking the root.
revision: The result equals the Euclidean length.

steps: Preallocate an output array.
Call `sqrt` with `out=` and print the buffer.
Confirm no new array was needed.
ufuncs accept out=.visual:
sqrt(a, out=out)
out holds the result
ufuncs accept out=.realWorld: Streaming pipelines reuse buffers to keep allocation out of the hot path.
mistakes: Passing an output with the wrong shape or dtype.

steps: Create a length-3 vector.
Broadcast it to a 2×3 shape.
Try to write into the result and observe the refusal.
broadcast_to makes the shape explicit.realWorld: Inspecting the effective shape of a broadcast prevents a wrong arithmetic assumption.
mistakes: Writing through a broadcast view.
revision: Zero strides mark the stretched axes.

steps: Create a (2, 3) matrix.
Multiply by a length-3 vector and print the shape.
Multiply by a (3, 2) matrix and read the error.
Trailing dimensions must match.realWorld: Feature scaling works because the parameter vector aligns with the last axis.
mistakes: Aligning shapes from the left instead of the right.
revision: Lengths must be equal or one.

steps: Create a matrix of values.
Sum each row with `keepdims=True`.
Divide the matrix by that column.
keepdims prepares a column for broadcast.realWorld: Normalising each sample by its own total is a keepdims division.
mistakes: Dropping the axis and getting a length mismatch.
revision: That shape broadcasts back against the input.

steps: Create a matrix.
Multiply it by a scalar.
Print the result and confirm every cell changed.
A matrix broadcasts with a scalar.realWorld: Converting units across a whole table is one scalar multiplication.
mistakes: Looping over cells when one operation is enough.
revision: A scalar has no axes to align.

steps: Create two vectors.
Turn the first into a column with `newaxis`.
Subtract the second and print the pairwise table.
Outer difference via newaxis.realWorld: A distance matrix between two sets of points starts as an outer difference.
mistakes: Leaving both vectors 1-D and producing a length mismatch.
revision: The result is the full outer table.

A broadcast error names the shapes.syntax: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes …
steps: Add two deliberately incompatible matrices.
Read the shapes in the error message.
Fix the axis with a reshape or transpose.
A broadcast error names the shapes.realWorld: Most shape bugs in a preprocessing pipeline surface as this one error.
mistakes: Reshaping blindly until the error disappears.
revision: Fix the axis that cannot stretch.

steps: Create a matrix.
Sum rows with and without keepdims.
Compare both shapes.
sum with keepdims keeps the axis.realWorld: A row total kept as a column can be divided straight back into the matrix.
mistakes: Forgetting that the default reduction deletes the axis.

steps: Create a small sorted array.
Ask for the median as 0.5.
Ask for the quartiles as a list.
quantile uses fractions.realWorld: Latency budgets are stated as p50 and p95 quantiles.
mistakes: Passing 50 instead of 0.5 to quantile.

steps: Create a matrix with distinct rows.
Find the best column per row.
Find the best row per column and compare.
argmax with an axis.visual:
axis=1 → one index per row
axis=0 → one index per column
argmax with an axis.realWorld: Argmax turns per-class scores into a predicted class index.
mistakes: Expecting argmax to return the maximum value.
revision: The axis argument selects what is reduced.

steps: Create a matrix.
Cumulatively sum each row.
Print the result and check the last cell equals the row total.
cumulative sum along a row.realWorld: Cumulative revenue or running totals are cumsum operations.
mistakes: Calling cumsum without an axis and flattening the matrix.
revision: The axis decides where it accumulates.

steps: Create values and matching weights.
Compute the weighted average.
Return the weight total with `returned=True`.
average accepts a weight per value.visual:
sum(w*x) / sum(w)
weights shift the centre
average accepts a weight per value.realWorld: Survey results are weighted by population so each group contributes fairly.
mistakes: Passing weights of the wrong length.
revision: The denominator is the weight total.

steps: Create a vector with a known range.
Compute `ptp`.
Compare it with max minus min.
ptp is max minus min.realWorld: Quality control reports the spread of a batch as its range.
mistakes: Using ptp with NaN values and getting NaN.

steps: Create a vector with zeros.
Call `nonzero` and print the index array.
Use the positions to select the values.
nonzero returns the positions.realWorld: Finding the set bits or non-zero features of a sparse row uses nonzero.
mistakes: Treating the tuple as a single index array.
revision: Nonzero returns one array per dimension.

steps: Create a matrix.
Build a threshold mask.
Sum the mask down the rows to count per column.
Count matches per column.realWorld: Missing-value counts per feature are a boolean sum down the rows.
mistakes: Summing without an axis and losing the per-column meaning.
revision: The named axis is the one collapsed.

steps: Create a vector of categories.
Build the membership mask with `isin`.
Filter the values with that mask.
Select with an isin mask.realWorld: Keeping only known country codes in a dataset is an isin filter.
mistakes: Using `in` inside a loop instead of a vectorised mask.
revision: The mask preserves the input shape.

steps: Create a matrix where the first column is a key.
Build a mask from that column.
Apply it to the matrix to keep whole rows.
Mask a matrix row-wise.realWorld: Filtering records by one field keeps the other fields attached.
mistakes: Applying a column mask to every cell instead of whole rows.
revision: The mask length must equal the row count.

steps: Create a condition and two value arrays.
Apply `where` and print the mix.
Swap the branches and compare.
where with two arrays.visual:
True → a, False → b
output shape is the broadcast shape
where with two arrays.realWorld: Replacing outliers with a capped value per cell is a where operation.
mistakes: Passing scalars when arrays were intended, then wondering about dtype.

steps: Create a vector.
Build two comparisons and combine them with `&`.
Filter with the combined mask.
Combine masks with and.realWorld: A price range filter is two conditions combined elementwise.
mistakes: Using Python `and`, which raises on arrays.

steps: Create an unsorted vector.
Sort it ascending.
Reverse the sorted result and print it.
sort descending by reversing.realWorld: Leaderboards show a descending sort of scores.
mistakes: Reversing before sorting and calling it descending.
revision: The reversal is a view of the sorted copy.

steps: Create a vector with repeats.
Ask for unique values and counts.
Pair the two arrays into a table.
unique with counts.realWorld: A value-count table for categories comes directly from unique with counts.
mistakes: Assuming first-seen order instead of sorted order.
revision: Counts align with the unique values.

steps: Create a sorted vector.
Find the insertion point for a value.
Try the same on an unsorted vector and inspect the meaningless result.
searchsorted needs a sorted array.realWorld: Bucket boundaries are located with a binary search over sorted edges.
mistakes: Calling searchsorted on data that was never sorted.

steps: Create an unsorted vector.
Partition at index k.
Verify the value at k is the k-th smallest and the sides are unordered.
partition with a kth position.realWorld: Top-k selection avoids a full sort when only the k-th value matters.
mistakes: Expecting both sides to be sorted.
revision: Partition guarantees only the k-th position.

steps: Create a primary and a secondary key.
Call `lexsort` with secondary first.
Apply the returned order to the data.
lexsort orders by two keys.visual:
sorts by primary,
ties broken by secondary
lexsort orders by two keys.realWorld: Sorting orders by date and then by customer id is a two-key lexsort.
mistakes: Passing the keys in the intuitive but wrong order.
revision: The last key is the primary key.

steps: Create a vector and an allowed set.
Call `isin` and print the mask.
Use the mask to filter the vector.
isin is membership testing.realWorld: Checking which IDs appear in a reference list is membership testing.
mistakes: Building a Python set and looping per element.

steps: Transpose a matrix to make it non-contiguous.
Print its C flag.
Convert it and print the flag again.
ascontiguousarray forces C order.realWorld: A C extension that requires contiguous input makes the copy visible here.
mistakes: Assuming the conversion always copies.

steps: Create an array.
Make it read-only.
Attempt an assignment and observe the error.
setflags can make an array read-only.realWorld: A shared configuration array is locked so a downstream function cannot mutate it.
mistakes: Believing another view of the buffer is also locked.
revision: The flag is per array object.

steps: Create an int32 array.
View it as uint8.
Compare the element counts and explain the difference.
view reinterprets the bytes.visual:
int32 2 elements
uint8 8 elements (4 bytes each)
view reinterprets the bytes.realWorld: Reading raw colour channels from packed pixels uses a dtype view.
mistakes: Using a view when a real numeric conversion was intended.
revision: A view changes interpretation, not bytes.

steps: Create an int16 matrix.
Print itemsize, size and nbytes.
Check that nbytes equals their product.
nbytes counts the whole buffer.realWorld: Memory budgeting for a batch starts from nbytes, not the element count.
mistakes: Confusing nbytes with the number of values.

steps: Create a vector.
Reverse it with a negative step.
Print the strides and compare with the source.
negative strides walk backwards.realWorld: Reversing a sequence for display costs no copy thanks to negative strides.
mistakes: Assuming a reversed slice copied the data.
revision: A negative step negates the stride.

steps: Copy an array.
Mutate the copy.
Print the source and check `shares_memory`.
copy is independent of the source.visual:
copy owns its buffer
shares_memory False
copy is independent of the source.realWorld: Passing a copy to a mutating helper protects the original dataset.
mistakes: Using a slice where a copy was needed.

steps: Create a seed sequence.
Spawn two child sequences.
Build a generator per child and compare their draws.
SeedSequence spawns independent streams.visual:
parent seed 42
→ child A, child B (independent)
SeedSequence spawns independent streams.realWorld: Parallel training workers need separate streams that stay reproducible from one seed.
mistakes: Sharing one generator across workers.
revision: The parent seed reproduces all of them.

steps: Create a default generator.
Draw values in a range.
Check the minimum and maximum are inside it.
uniform takes low and high.realWorld: Random initial weights are drawn from a small uniform range.
mistakes: Assuming the high bound can be returned.

steps: Draw integers with a narrow dtype.
Print the dtype and values.
Request a range that does not fit and read the error.
integers can take a dtype.realWorld: Compact label arrays save memory when the category count is small.
mistakes: Requesting a range wider than the chosen dtype.
revision: The dtype is applied to the draw.

steps: Draw a sample with a chosen mean and standard deviation.
Print the sample mean and std.
Change the scale and repeat.
normal takes mean and std.visual:
loc centres the draws
scale widens them
normal takes mean and std.realWorld: Synthetic measurement noise is generated with a mean and a standard deviation.
mistakes: Passing variance where the standard deviation is expected.

steps: Create a vector.
Shuffle it with a generator.
Print the array and note the missing return value.
shuffle works in place.visual:
shuffle(a) → None
a itself is reordered
shuffle works in place.realWorld: Shuffling a dataset in place before splitting is a common step.
mistakes: Assigning the return value and getting None.

steps: Define values and matching probabilities.
Draw a sample with `p=`.
Check the probabilities sum to one.
choice takes probabilities.visual:
p=[0.9, 0.1]
0 is drawn about nine times as often
choice takes probabilities.realWorld: Sampling a class imbalance with weights uses choice with probabilities.
mistakes: Passing unnormalised probabilities.

steps: Create a date and print its dtype.
Add a one-day timedelta.
Print the result and confirm the unit.
datetime64 carries its unit.realWorld: Daily sales dates are stored as datetime64[D] so arithmetic stays in whole days.
mistakes: Adding a bare number without a unit.
